'''Hazel L. Sive''' is a [[South Africa|South African]] scientist. She currently serves as Dean of the College of Science and Mathematics at the University of Massachusetts.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Boston |first=UMass |title=Dean's Office - UMass Boston |url=https://www.umb.edu/science-mathematics/deans-office/ |access-date=2026-01-08 |website=www.umb.edu |language=en}}</ref> Sive's research includes studies of neurological and [[neurodevelopmental disorder]]s, such as [[epilepsy]], [[autism]], and 16p11.2 deletion syndrome.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sivelab.wi.mit.edu/research/|title=Research {{!}} Sive Lab|website=sivelab.wi.mit.edu|language=en-US|access-date=2018-09-07}}</ref>

==Education==
Sive received her [[Bachelor of Science]] with honors in 1979 from the [[University of the Witwatersrand]] in [[Johannesburg]], [[South Africa]] with a double major in zoology and chemistry.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://ocw.mit.edu/faculty/hazel-sive/|title=Hazel Sive {{!}} MIT OpenCourseWare {{!}} Free Online Course Materials|last=OpenCourseWare|first=MIT|website=ocw.mit.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-11-26}}</ref>{{Dead link|date=July 2026}}{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} 

==Research==
{{Technical|date=July 2026|section}}
Sive's research includes analysis of the extreme anterior domain (EAD), a region found in developing embryos that develops into the mouth opening and oral cavity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jacox |first1=Laura A. |last2=Dickinson |first2=Amanda J. |last3=Sive |first3=Hazel |title=Facial Transplants in ''Xenopus laevis'' Embryos |journal=Journal of Visualized Experiments |date=26 March 2014 |issue=85 |doi=10.3791/50697|pmid=24748020 |pmc=4089428 }}</ref> This research defined key steps of mouth formation and determined that the EAD is a facial [[Developmental signaling center|signaling center]] that guides [[neural crest]] cells into the developing face, where they form the jaws and other structures.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jacox |first1=Laura |last2=Chen |first2=Justin |last3=Rothman |first3=Alyssa |last4=Lathrop-Marshall |first4=Hillary |last5=Sive |first5=Hazel |title=Formation of a "Pre-mouth Array" from the Extreme Anterior Domain Is Directed by Neural Crest and Wnt/PCP Signaling |journal=Cell Reports |date=August 2016 |volume=16 |issue=5 |pages=1445–1455 |doi=10.1016/j.celrep.2016.06.073|pmid=27425611 |pmc=4972695 }}</ref>

Sive has conducted research into nervous system patterning.{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} She was involved in the development of subtractive cloning techniques used to define nervous system molecular markers and regulators in ''[[Xenopus]]'' frogs and the zebrafish ''[[Danio]]''. Expression of these genes determine the point at which an embryo begins to develop a nervous system: Sive determined that future brain cells are set aside when the embryo is just a ball of cells.{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} Sive was the first to use hormone-inducible fusion proteins to study these genes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kolm |first1=Peggy J. |last2=Sive |first2=Hazel L. |title=Efficient Hormone-Inducible Protein Function in Xenopus laevis |journal=Developmental Biology |date=September 1995 |volume=171 |issue=1 |pages=267–272 |doi=10.1006/dbio.1995.1279|pmid=7556904 |doi-access=free }}</ref> 

Sive developed the first [[zebrafish]] 'explant' culture method, and identified cell interactions that initiate brain development.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sagerström |first1=C. G. |last2=Grinblat |first2=Y. |last3=Sive |first3=H. |title=Anteroposterior patterning in the zebrafish, Danio rerio: an explant assay reveals inductive and suppressive cell interactions |journal=Development |date=June 1996 |volume=122 |issue=6 |pages=1873–1883 |doi=10.1242/dev.122.6.1873 |issn=0950-1991|pmid=8674426 }}</ref> Sive identified [[retinoic acid]] as a regulator of brain patterning, and demonstrated its activity on expression of [[hindbrain]] Hox genes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kolm |first1=Peggy J. |last2=Sive |first2=Hazel L. |title=Regulation of the Xenopus labial Homeodomain Genes, HoxA1 and HoxD1: Activation by Retinoids and Peptide Growth Factors |journal=Developmental Biology |date=January 1995 |volume=167 |issue=1 |pages=34–49 |doi=10.1006/dbio.1995.1005|pmid=7851655 |doi-access=free }}</ref> She defined additional roles for [[fibroblast]] growth factors in precise patterning of the hindbrain.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kolm |first1=Peggy J. |last2=Apekin |first2=Vladimir |last3=Sive |first3=Hazel |title=XenopusHindbrain Patterning Requires Retinoid Signaling |journal=Developmental Biology |date=December 1997 |volume=192 |issue=1 |pages=1–16 |doi=10.1006/dbio.1997.8754|pmid=9405093 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Sive was instrumental in the identification of "basal constriction" as a cell-shape-change occurring during brain morphogenesis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gutzman |first1=Jennifer H. |last2=Graeden |first2=Ellie G. |last3=Lowery |first3=Laura Anne |last4=Holley |first4=Heidi S. |last5=Sive |first5=Hazel |title=Formation of the zebrafish midbrain–hindbrain boundary constriction requires laminin-dependent basal constriction |journal=Mechanisms of Development |date=November 2008 |volume=125 |issue=11–12 |pages=974–983 |doi=10.1016/j.mod.2008.07.004|pmid=18682291 |pmc=2780020 }}</ref> They identified the process of "epithelial relaxation," a cell-sheet-stretching process that occurs as brain ventricles form.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gutzman |first1=J. H. |last2=Sive |first2=H. |title=Epithelial relaxation mediated by the myosin phosphatase regulator Mypt1 is required for brain ventricle lumen expansion and hindbrain morphogenesis |journal=Development |date=10 February 2010 |volume=137 |issue=5 |pages=795–804 |doi=10.1242/dev.042705|pmid=20147380 |pmc=2827689 }}</ref> She was one of the first to use zebrafish to study the brain ventricular system: cavities filled with [[cerebrospinal fluid]] (CSF) that form the body's "third circulation."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lowery |first1=L. A. |title=Initial formation of zebrafish brain ventricles occurs independently of circulation and requires the nagie oko and snakehead/atp1a1a.1 gene products |journal=Development |date=23 March 2005 |volume=132 |issue=9 |pages=2057–2067 |doi=10.1242/dev.01791|pmid=15788456 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This research identified [[Retinol]] Binding Protein in the CSF as essential for the survival of brain cells.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=Jessica T. |last2=Lehtinen |first2=Maria K. |last3=Sive |first3=Hazel |title=Zebrafish cerebrospinal fluid mediates cell survival through a retinoid signaling pathway |journal=Developmental Neurobiology |date=January 2016 |volume=76 |issue=1 |pages=75–92 |doi=10.1002/dneu.22300|pmid=25980532 |pmc=4644717 }}</ref>

Sive investigated zebrafish as a tool for probing gene function associated with autism spectrum disorders.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tropepe |first1=V |last2=Sive |first2=HL |title=Can zebrafish be used as a model to study the neurodevelopmental causes of autism? |journal=Genes, Brain and Behavior |date=October 2003 |volume=2 |issue=5 |pages=268–81 |pmid=14606692|doi=10.1034/j.1601-183X.2003.00038.x |doi-access=free }}</ref> Her group has identified genes that interact and contribute to brain dysfunction in the prevalent and serious 16p11.2 deletion syndrome, implicating lipid metabolism in symptomatology.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Blaker-Lee |first1=A. |last2=Gupta |first2=S. |last3=McCammon |first3=J. M. |last4=De Rienzo |first4=G. |last5=Sive |first5=H. |title=Zebrafish homologs of genes within 16p11.2, a genomic region associated with brain disorders, are active during brain development, and include two deletion dosage sensor genes |journal=Disease Models & Mechanisms |date=1 May 2012 |volume=5 |issue=6 |pages=834–851 |doi=10.1242/dmm.009944 |doi-access=free|pmid=22566537 |pmc=3484866 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=McCammon |first1=Jasmine M. |last2=Blaker-Lee |first2=Alicia |last3=Chen |first3=Xiao |last4=Sive |first4=Hazel |title=The 16p11.2 homologs fam57ba and doc2a generate certain brain and body phenotypes |journal=Human Molecular Genetics |date=1 October 2017 |volume=26 |issue=19 |pages=3699–3712 |doi=10.1093/hmg/ddx255|pmid=28934389 |pmc=5886277 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tomasello |first=Danielle L. |last2=Kim |first2=Jiyoon L. |last3=Khodour |first3=Yara |last4=McCammon |first4=Jasmine M. |last5=Mitalipova |first5=Maya |last6=Jaenisch |first6=Rudolf |last7=Futerman |first7=Anthony H. |last8=Sive |first8=Hazel |date=2022-01-21 |title=16pdel lipid changes in iPSC-derived neurons and function of FAM57B in lipid metabolism and synaptogenesis |journal=iScience |volume=25 |issue=1 |article-number=103551 |doi=10.1016/j.isci.2021.103551 |issn=2589-0042 |pmc=8693007 |pmid=34984324}}</ref>

Sive is the editor of ''Xenopus: A Laboratory Manual.''<ref>{{Cite book |title=Xenopus: a laboratory manual |date=2023 |publisher=Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press |isbn=978-1-62182-180-9 |editor-last=Sive |editor-first=Hazel L. |location=Cold Spring Harbor, New York}}</ref>

==Academic roles and awards==
In 2015, she was named a MacVicar Faculty Fellow, MIT's highest award for undergraduate teaching<ref>{{cite web|title=Current MacVicar Fellows|url=https://registrar.mit.edu/faculty-curriculum-support/faculty-awards/margaret-macvicar-faculty-fellows-program/macvicar-fellows/current|website=MIT Registrar's Office}}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=July 2026|reason=does not provide evidence of Hazel Sive as a MacVicar Faculty Fellow}}.

She received the MIT School of Science Teaching Award (2003), MIT's Alan J. Lazarus Advising Award in 2016, and the MIS School of Science Teaching Award for Undergraduate Education in 2019.<ref>{{cite web |title=Teaching prize recipients |url=https://science.mit.edu/about/awards/science-teaching-prizes/teaching-prize-recipients/ |website=MIT School of Science |access-date=21 February 2019 |archive-date=30 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190730094646/https://science.mit.edu/about/awards/science-teaching-prizes/teaching-prize-recipients/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Office of Undergraduate Advising & Academic Programming {{!}} Awards Convocation |url=http://awards.mit.edu/institute-awards/2015-2016-awards/office-undergraduate-advising-academic-programming |website=awards.mit.edu}}</ref>{{Dead link|date=July 2026}}<ref>{{cite web |title=Mehrdad Jazayeri and Hazel Sive awarded 2019 School of Science teaching prizes |date=18 September 2019 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2019/jazayeri-sive-awarded-school-science-teaching-prizes-0918}}</ref> Several of her courses are offered through the MIT OpenCourseWare online initiative.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hazel Sive {{!}} MIT OpenCourseWare {{!}} Free Online Course Materials |url=https://ocw.mit.edu/faculty/hazel-sive/ |website=ocw.mit.edu |language=en}}</ref>{{Dead link|date=July 2026}}{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}

Sive was chair of the MIT Biology Undergraduate Program (2003–2006) and served as the first Associate Dean for the MIT School of Science (2006–2013).<ref name="assoc_dean">{{cite web |title=Hazel Sive steps down as associate dean of the School of Science |url=https://news.mit.edu/2013/hazel-sive-steps-down-as-associate-dean-of-the-school-of-science |website=MIT News|date=20 December 2013 }}</ref>  

Sive has served as chair of the MIT Committee on Student Life and as founding chair of the MIT Faculty Postdoctoral Advisory Committee.<ref name="jwel">{{cite web |title=Professor Hazel Sive |url=https://jwel.mit.edu/staff/professor-hazel-sive |website=MIT J-WEL |language=en |date=2 March 2018}}</ref>{{Dead link|date=July 2026}}{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}

In 2014, Sive founded and is Director of the MIT-Africa initiative, leading the Africa Advisory Committee to write a Strategic Plan for MIT Engagement in Africa.<ref>{{cite web |title=What is MIT-Africa? |url=https://africa.mit.edu/what-is-mit-africa/ |website=MIT Africa}}</ref>{{Dead link|date=July 2026}}{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}

In 2017, Sive was named Director of Higher Education at the MIT Jameel World Education Lab (J-WEL).<ref name="jwel" />{{Dead link|date=July 2026}}{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}

She was formerly a Member of the Whitehead Institute<ref>{{cite web |title=Alumni, Whitehead Institute: Hazel L. Sive |url=https://wi.mit.edu/people/alumni/sive |website=wi.mit.edu}}</ref> and joined the MIT faculty in 1991.<ref>{{cite web |title=OCW Faculty Profile: Hazel Sive |url=https://ocw.mit.edu/faculty/hazel-sive/ |website=ocw.mit.edu}}</ref> 

In November 2021, she was elected as an AAAS Fellow.<ref>{{cite web|title=2021 AAAS Fellows|url=https://www.aaas.org/page/2021-fellows}}</ref> Sive received the recognition for fundamental discoveries advancing our understanding of early embryonic development, particularly the [[development of the nervous system]] in vertebrates, and for her leadership in teaching, mentoring, and diversity in higher education.<ref>{{cite web|title=Three Northeastern Leaders Receive Lifetime Honor for Prolific Scientific Contribution|date=27 January 2022 |url=https://news.northeastern.edu/2022/01/27/aaas-fellowship-awards/}}</ref>

In 2022, Sive was awarded an honorary doctorate in engineering from her alma mater, the University of the Witwatersrand.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lloyd |first=Noah |date=December 12, 2022 |title=The door doesn't close on learning: Dean Hazel Sive receives honorary doctorate |work=Northeastern Global News |url=https://news.northeastern.edu/research/archives/the-door-doesnt-close-on-learning-dean-hazel-sive-receives-honorary-doctorate/ |access-date=August 15, 2023}}</ref>
